title: Why Heat Is Becoming A Bigger Chip Design Issue
gist: A DAC roundtable of EDA vendors (Synopsys, Silvaco, Vinci, Keysight, Siemens) argues heat is now a system-level problem requiring coupled thermal, electrical and timing analysis, for which no single tool exists yet. They expect full 3D-IC to arrive with costly cooling and materials work, and look to agentic AI to break discipline silos.

insights.claim: Lowering voltage cuts heat but changes timing and performance, so designers must find a sweet spot via a closed loop of timing, thermal and power-integrity co-optimization across multiple workloads; no tool yet does this whole loop.
insights.speaker: Lang Lin (Synopsys)
insights.so_what: An unaddressed multi-physics workflow gap is an opportunity for EDA vendors who integrate it first.
insights.quote: We don’t have a tool yet to do this big loop
insights.locator: SE: One of the big trade-offs

insights.claim: Temperature changes resistance, which changes current and power, which changes temperature, so simulation must be fully coupled; the speaker expects the industry's focus to go there, probably starting next year.
insights.speaker: Satish Radhakrishnan (Vinci)
insights.so_what: Coupled electro-thermal sign-off becomes a competitive requirement for EDA toolchains in 2027.
insights.quote: All of this is going to be coupled, probably starting next year.

insights.claim: Thermal time constants differ from the speed of electrons through a transistor, a disconnect that must be consistently accounted for in design, especially with new materials.
insights.speaker: Jack Berg (Silvaco)
insights.so_what: Multi-timescale modeling is a core technical challenge for thermal-aware design.

insights.claim: Complex designs must now analyze voltage, timing, resistance, power and temperature together and in context of each other, and thermal is a system-level problem.
insights.speaker: Ed Sperling
insights.so_what: Siloed point tools become less useful as thermal couples with all other domains.

insights.claim: Vendors on the panel treat full 3D-IC as a question of when, not if, requiring more materials-science investment, with exotic options like stacked intercoolers with fluid circulation that would be incredibly expensive and reserved for high-performance applications.
insights.speaker: Chris Mueth (Keysight)
insights.so_what: Cost of advanced cooling will confine true 3D-IC to premium AI/HPC segments initially.

insights.claim: Cooled interposers are one thermal technique but the industry is heading toward fully stacked 3D-IC with optics coming in on the side; it will be more expensive, so it may need to start with a narrow application.
insights.speaker: Satish Radhakrishnan (Vinci)
insights.so_what: Narrow initial applications imply limited near-term volume for full 3D-IC.

insights.claim: By definition, a stack of 16 HBMs in one package is already a 3D-IC, and further z-level scaling will need materials scientists with thermal and mechanical skills; hybrid bonding and nanometer-scale TSVs are enabling it.
insights.speaker: Jack Berg (Silvaco)
insights.so_what: Hybrid bonding and TSV scaling are the enabling technologies to track for vertical integration.

insights.claim: Heterogeneous technology integration, matching the right technology to each function, can help super-high-performance applications that need small size.
insights.speaker: Chris Mueth (Keysight)
insights.so_what: Heterogeneous integration is a thermal lever as well as a performance one.

insights.claim: Siemens' Ferguson compares today's thermal doubts to early Moore's Law, where each node was declared impossible yet arrived, though later than wanted, and warns that uncoordinated efforts (thermal vs materials chemistry changes) could collide at the wrong time.
insights.speaker: John Ferguson (Siemens EDA)
insights.so_what: Ecosystem coordination, formerly via ITRS, is now seen as the bigger risk than physics itself.

insights.claim: Agents let place-and-route engineers check thermal themselves via natural language (e.g. asking for Tmax), replacing the old model where designs were sent to a separate thermal team.
insights.speaker: Lang Lin (Synopsys)
insights.so_what: EDA agents erode specialist-team bottlenecks, changing team structure and tool-seat economics.

insights.claim: Keysight's Mueth says AI has advanced astonishingly in the past year, citing a hackathon where tools did things never thought possible, and says customers will want to drive orchestration themselves.
insights.speaker: Chris Mueth (Keysight)
insights.so_what: Vendors position as enablers of customer-owned orchestration, not black-box automation.

insights.claim: Single-domain engineers must now handle multi-domain problems, achievable via AI or by simplifying multi-physics offerings so single-domain users can run them.
insights.speaker: Chris Mueth (Keysight)
insights.so_what: Two vendor strategies emerge: AI agents versus dumbed-down multi-physics.

insights.claim: AI used for design decisions must be accurate because a wrong answer leads to a wrong design, and it must connect mechanical, electrical and other teams.
insights.speaker: Satish Radhakrishnan (Vinci)
insights.so_what: Accuracy and trust, not capability, will gate adoption of AI in sign-off flows.

insights.claim: Ferguson says Model Context Protocols can run tasks far faster than people, and the industry needs people to find and build the right MCPs.
insights.speaker: John Ferguson (Siemens EDA)
insights.so_what: MCP is emerging as an EDA integration layer, creating a new skill and vendor-lock-in axis.

insights.claim: Mixing CPUs, GPUs and accelerators for agentic AI is harder to manage but yields efficiency, and efficiency translates to better thermal and electrical performance, a trade of design complexity against performance.
insights.speaker: Chris Mueth (Keysight)
insights.so_what: Heterogeneous compute is a thermal strategy, supporting multi-silicon vendor demand.

insights.claim: In multi-physics EDA, GPUs matter because 3D matrix solving parallelizes well; Synopsys envisions thousands of GPUs solving partitions of a 3D-IC with CPUs orchestrating and reasoning.
insights.speaker: Lang Lin (Synopsys)
insights.so_what: EDA itself becomes a GPU-demand source beyond AI training.

insights.claim: Large GPU banks can generate synthetic data from cross-coupled physics solvers to build surrogate models that run on ordinary CPUs for what-if analysis, provided physics is calibrated to data and interpolation is distinguished from extrapolation.
insights.speaker: Jack Berg (Silvaco)
insights.so_what: Surrogate models democratize thermal what-ifs but their validity bounds are a risk.
